post.text:
lol what: Researchers found that repeating the exact same prompt twice dramatically improves LLM performance (one model improved from 21% to 97% accuracy on a name-search task) without longer outputs, slower responses, fine-tuning, or fancy prompt engineering.

Because models process text left to right, duplicating the input gives every token a second chance to “see” the full context, leading to measurable gains across 7 benchmarks and 7 major models.

Edit: ofc for NON-REASONING

comments.name: CRISPRKing
comments.text:
Transformer models process tokens sequentially building representations layer by layer. Early tokens have less context than later ones because they can't look ahead. Repeating input essentially gives model second pass where later processing benefits from fuller context.

The improvement from 21% to 97% is suspiciously dramatic and probably task-specific. Most benchmarks won't see that magnitude improvement from simple duplication. But modest gains are plausible because second pass allows deeper processing of relationships that first pass missed.

Practical limitation is this doubles token count and therefore cost. For API users paying per token, repeating everything costs 2x. The tradeoff between accuracy and cost only makes sense for high-value queries where correctness is worth double price.

This feels like quirk of current architecture rather than fundamental principle. Future model designs might handle bidirectional context better or use recurrent processing that doesn't need duplication. Exploiting the quirk works now but probably gets optimized away in next generation architectures.
